title: Introduce database performance regression
description: Project: Introduce database performance regression. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: Database performance regressions often arrive quietly: a query that used to take 20ms now takes 800ms, and the first signal is a user complaint rather than an alert. This lesson introduces common regression patterns in relational databases, how to recognize them from query plans, and what architectural defenses prevent them from reaching production.

items: N+1 queries hidden inside loops or lazy-loaded navigation properties
Missing indexes on columns used in WHERE, JOIN, or ORDER BY clauses
Implicit conversions that prevent index seeks and force table scans
Lock escalation or deadlocks caused by long-running transactions
Parameter sniffing where a cached plan optimized for one parameter value is poor for others
Connection pool exhaustion under load, causing queuing rather than query slowness

terms.definition: The execution strategy a database optimizer chooses for a statement, including index seeks, scans, joins, and sorts.
A lookup that navigates directly to matching rows using a B-tree; much faster than scanning every row.
A pattern where one query fetches a parent collection, then N additional queries fetch each child individually.
When SQL Server caches a plan based on the first parameter value, which may be atypical for subsequent executions.
A cache of open database connections reused by an application to avoid the overhead of creating new connections.

data.text: The fastest query is the one you do not run. Before optimizing a slow query, ask whether it needs to run at all. Can the result be cached? Can the request be precomputed? Can the user request fewer rows? Eliminating work is more durable than making work faster.

data.title: N+1 query pattern in EF Core
data.content: Lazy loading inside a loop causes N+1 queries. Use Include or a projection instead:

items: Capture the slow query with an execution plan or extended events session
Look for scans, key lookups, and spills to tempdb as primary red flags
Compare the actual plan to the estimated plan to identify parameter sniffing
Check index usage statistics to confirm the index exists and is being used
Run the query under production-like data volume to confirm the fix holds

cards.title: Add an index
cards.description: Create a B-tree index on filtered or sorted columns.
cons: Can become unused and need maintenance

cards.title: Rewrite the query
cards.description: Restructure joins, projections, or pagination to reduce work.

cards.title: Introduce caching
cards.description: Cache hot query results in Redis or memory.

data.title: Indexes are not free
data.text: Every index speeds up reads and slows down writes. Adding an index to a table with high INSERT volume can increase write latency noticeably. Monitor write latency after adding any index, and drop indexes that are not used.

items: Run query plan analysis in CI for any migration that changes schema or adds queries
Set up automated index usage monitoring to catch unused indexes before they bloat storage
Use read replicas for reporting queries to isolate analytical load from transactional workloads
Cap long-running queries with a statement timeout to prevent cascading saturation

data.title: Diagnose a slow query
data.description: You are given a query that runs in 800ms on production but 20ms on development. The execution plan shows a clustered index scan. Identify the likely causes and propose a fix.
steps: Compare the data volume between dev and production environments
Check whether statistics are up to date on production
Look for implicit column conversions in the WHERE clause
Propose an index or query rewrite and justify the choice
data.expectedOutcome: You should be able to explain why the plan differs between environments and propose a fix that works at production scale.

data.title: Summary
points: Start with the execution plan, not the query text
Eliminate N+1 before tuning individual queries
Indexes help reads but hurt writes; balance both
Validate fixes under production-like data volume
Prevent regressions with CI-based query plan analysis
data.takeaway: A senior engineer treats database performance as a continuous responsibility, not a one-time optimization task. Instrumentation, review, and periodic audits keep regressions from reaching users.
